article.overview: Laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS) is a remote or close-range elemental analysis technique. A pulsed laser is focused onto a small spot on a target, vaporising a tiny amount of material and forming a hot plasma. As the plasma cools, the atoms and ions in it emit light at element-specific wavelengths, which a spectrometer records. The class is defined by its measurement principle rather than by one design, and this article covers LIBS instruments that perform elemental analysis of surface targets by laser-plasma emission spectroscopy. Examples reviewed: ChemCam on NASA's Curiosity rover (flown and operated on Mars); SuperCam on NASA's Perseverance rover (flown and operated on Mars); MarSCoDe on China's Zhurong rover (flown; Zhurong LIBS data reported in a 2022 supplementary information file); the Chandrayaan-2 rover LIBS (flight model built and integrated into the rover, but the lander was lost and surface operation is not reported); and the Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover LIBS (reported by ISRO as operated on the lunar surface in 2023). Scope: in scope are the LIBS instruments and their laser, optics, collection, spectrometer and calibration aspects. Cross-referenced and not duplicated: catalogue 054 (Alpha Particle X-ray Spectrometer, APXS, which shared the Chandrayaan-3 rover with LIBS), 055 (X-ray fluorescence spectrometer), 063 (Raman spectrometer; SuperCam's Raman mode is mentioned only as a companion), 066 (laser ablation instrument), 074 (laser-induced fluorescence spectrometer) and 075 (laser-induced plasma spectrometer; the boundary between 060 and 075 is not decided here). Excluded: lunar landing-site recommendations and lander or rover compatibility claims without verified interface evidence.
article.description: A LIBS instrument typically has four functional parts. A pulsed laser, usually a solid-state laser emitting short near-infrared pulses, delivers energy to the target. An optical train focuses the beam onto the target and, in remote designs, uses a telescope to do so from metres away. A collection system gathers plasma light and sends it to the spectrometer through an optical fibre or mirrors. A spectrometer and detector resolve the light by wavelength and convert it to an electronic spectrum. Remote LIBS uses a telescope at a standoff distance of metres (ChemCam and SuperCam are remote designs). The Chandrayaan-2 rover LIBS is a close-range design with a fixed instrument-to-surface distance of 205 mm. LIBS can detect many major rock-forming elements in a single laser shot. Emission lines from hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, sulphur and phosphorus are harder to measure. The Chandrayaan-2 paper lists detection of these volatile and trace elements as scientific aims rather than established capabilities of that instrument. ISRO states that hydrogen detection on the Chandrayaan-3 rover was still under investigation at the time of its announcement.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose of a lunar LIBS is in situ elemental analysis of surface material. Chemical composition helps show how lunar soils and rocks formed, because soil chemistry reflects the underlying bedrock and can differ between geologically distinct areas. The Chandrayaan-2 paper states that comparing soil chemistry from widely separated landing sites, or from distinct areas around one site, can give insight into regolith formation. The Chandrayaan-2 paper lists the rock-forming elements the instrument was intended to detect: O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, K, Ca, Fe, Cr, Mn and Ti, together with volatile and trace elements H, C, N, S and P in the vicinity of the landing site. These are published design aims, not measured results. ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 LIBS announcement (28 August 2023) reports aluminium, sulphur, calcium, iron, chromium and titanium as preliminary findings, with manganese, silicon and oxygen added in later measurements and hydrogen still under investigation. Spectroscopy Online reports that the APXS on the same rover also detected sulphur. The sources reviewed do not provide the quantitative analysis or uncertainties behind the ISRO element list. On Mars, LIBS instruments have analysed rocks and soils across many targets. A secondary summary indexed during research states that the ChemCam team used its laser and spectrometers on more than 600 rock or soil targets in its first two years on Mars. This count was not verified in a primary mission paper and is not used as a numerical specification.
article.operating_principle: LIBS works in four steps. (1) Ablation: a short, high-energy laser pulse strikes the target and heats the surface so strongly that a small amount of material is vaporised, atomised and ionised. (2) Plasma formation: the result is a glowing cloud of excited atoms, ions and electrons. The Chandrayaan-2 paper describes a relaxation time of typically a few tens of microseconds before the emission has largely decayed. (3) Light collection: a telescope, lens-mirror arrangement or fibre collects light from the plasma and sends it to the spectrometer, which disperses the light by wavelength (usually with a grating) and a detector records it. (4) Analysis: each element emits at characteristic wavelengths. Line intensity depends on abundance but also on the target matrix, laser energy and instrument response, so quantitative results need calibration against reference materials measured with the same instrument. Operating modes differ between instruments. The Chandrayaan-2 paper describes modes that capture plasma emission after the last laser shot, after each shot, or for a single shot. Repeated shots at the same spot can progressively penetrate dust on a rock's surface, as NASA's ChemCam image of the rock Nova shows.
article.scientific_importance: LIBS is important for lunar science because it gives rapid, element-by-element information about surface material at the scale of the laser spot, without sample collection. This complements orbital measurements, which cannot always confirm that an element is present at the surface. ISRO states that the Chandrayaan-3 LIBS measurements confirmed sulphur near the south pole in a way that orbiter instruments could not. On Mars, LIBS has shown that a remote laser can produce useful composition data on rocks and soils at distances of metres. SuperCam's LIBS standoff extends to 7 m, and the SuperCam Body Unit paper states that SuperCam has the same distance capability as ChemCam. The technique's limits, including small spot size, near-surface sampling and matrix dependence, shape the interpretation of its results (see limitations).

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a LIBS payload. The examples differ in laser wavelength, pulse energy, distance, spectrometer design, platform and status, so their values are not directly comparable and no combined table is given for LIBS as a class. Where a value is not published in the sources reviewed it is stated as null or 'not publicly specified'. Mass and power figures are shown only where the source ties them to a named instrument or subsystem.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions vary widely across the examples. The Chandrayaan-2 LIBS has a volume of 180 x 150 x 80 mm (Table 1) and a fixed instrument-to-surface distance of 205 mm. The SuperCam Mast Unit measures 383 x 201 x 163 mm and the Body Unit 221 x 157 x 205 mm, but these are whole-hardware values including non-LIBS subsystems. ChemCam's Mast Unit telescope has a 110 mm primary mirror. The MarSCoDe LIBS dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources read. Dimensions are not comparable across these designs and must be tied to named instruments.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: The Chandrayaan-2 LIBS mass is about 1.1 kg (abstract and Table 1) with a 1.2 kg requirement stated in the introduction. The SuperCam whole-hardware masses are 6.11 kg (Mast Unit), 4.44 kg (Body Unit), 0.25 kg (calibration target) and 10.80 kg (total), and these are not LIBS-only masses. ChemCam and MarSCoDe LIBS masses are not publicly specified in the sources read. The Chandrayaan-3 LIBS mass is not publicly specified.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: The Chandrayaan-2 LIBS draws 1.19 W in steady state and a peak of 10.42 W for 20 shots at 5 Hz with the laser on. The SuperCam totals are 27 W maximum for the Mast Unit, 43 W maximum for the Body Unit including thermo-electric cooler operation, 12 W idle for the Body Unit, and 70 W total for the hardware as stated in the Body Unit paper. ChemCam, MarSCoDe and Chandrayaan-3 LIBS power values are not publicly specified in the sources read. The MarSCoDe secondary summaries mention solar power limits, which have not been verified.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: On the lunar surface, the Chandrayaan-2 paper defines a design requirement of -60 to -90 C, operating limits of -20 to +55 C and storage limits of -40 to +70 C. The Moon has no atmosphere to shield the optics, so thermal, vacuum and dust effects are significant. On Mars, the ChemCam laser needs warm-up before use and has a preferred temperature range; SuperCam's remote sensing electronics box has a survival temperature above -40 C. Common operational needs for remote and close-range LIBS include maintaining focus at the expected standoff distance, dealing with dust that changes the spectrum, keeping the laser within its energy limits, accounting for surface modification by repeated shots, and collecting plasma light within the spectrometer's wavelength range and resolution. Standard engineering considerations for power, thermal control and data handling apply, but no source reviewed gives a verified interface for a named lunar lander or rover.
article.limitations: LIBS has several limitations across the examples. Spot size: the analysed volume is small (about 0.06-0.55 mm across the examples), so the analysis reflects a small surface patch and heterogeneous material may be unrepresentative. Calibration and matrix effects: quantitative results depend on calibration against reference materials. SuperCam uses a library of 332 standards; the Chandrayaan-2 paper describes calibration with standard and certified reference soil powders under vacuum. The Chandrayaan-3 calibration accuracy is not given in the sources read. Light elements and volatiles: hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and related elements are harder to detect quantitatively; ISRO reports hydrogen detection on Chandrayaan-3 as under investigation. Surface and dust effects: dust, weathering and surface roughness change the plasma and the spectrum, and repeated shots can modify the surface. Thermal and power constraints: lunar night and extreme temperatures constrain the instrument (the Chandrayaan-2 design considered -60 to -90 C). Evidence limitations: the lunar examples rest on one peer-reviewed paper about an instrument that did not operate on the surface and on ISRO and press announcements for Chandrayaan-3.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: LIBS on the Moon is a surface instrument. It requires a stable platform that can place the optics at a known distance from the target and point them at the surface. The Chandrayaan-2 LIBS was designed to be mounted on the rover's chassis with its optical head pointing at the lunar surface at a fixed investigation distance of 205 mm. Remote LIBS on Mars is mounted on rovers (SuperCam on the Perseverance remote sensing mast; MarSCoDe described as on the Zhurong front deck in secondary sources). Orbiter-only LIBS is not a conventional design because LIBS needs close-range access to a surface target. Sample-return integration is not applicable.
transportation_process: Integrate the LIBS into the rover (or lander) on Earth, including optics alignment and the rover interface.
Launch the spacecraft with the rover or lander on a launch vehicle.
Transfer the spacecraft to the Moon.
Deliver the rover or lander to the surface, which requires a surface-capable carrier.
Deploy the rover, where mobility is used to reach targets, and point the LIBS optics at the surface target.
Connect the instrument to rover power and data systems (the Chandrayaan-2 paper describes a 16-bit serial tele-command interface and checkout to the rover interface).
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: The LIBS is rover-mounted. Chandrayaan-2 planned a fixed investigation distance and pointing at the surface; it did not describe a separate deployment mechanism for the LIBS. The Chandrayaan-2 lander was the intended carrier, but its loss means the rover interface was not tested on the surface. No compatibility with a specific lander or rover is asserted.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: ChemCam (Curiosity), SuperCam (Perseverance) and MarSCoDe (Zhurong) are Mars rover LIBS examples. The Chandrayaan-2 rover LIBS was built and integrated but the lander was lost. The Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover LIBS is reported as operated on the lunar surface.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No verified interface evidence for a named lunar lander or rover was reviewed. Compatibility would need comparison of mass, dimensions, mounting, field of view, pointing, power, thermal and data interfaces against verified spacecraft specifications. This article does not assign LIBS to any lander.

article.historical_significance: LIBS has a flight history on Mars that began with ChemCam on Curiosity, described in the Chandrayaan-2 paper as the first space-based LIBS instrument flown to Mars. SuperCam and MarSCoDe extended the approach to the Perseverance and Zhurong rovers. On the Moon, the Chandrayaan-2 LIBS was a significant engineering milestone because it was built for a lunar rover, qualified and integrated, but did not operate on the surface after the lander was lost. ISRO reports that the Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan rover LIBS made the first in-situ elemental analysis by LIBS of the lunar surface near the south pole, confirming sulphur. These statements rely on ISRO's announcement and press coverage and should be checked against any future peer-reviewed or technical publication.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: ChemCam laser values conflict across sources (pulse energy above 10 mJ on the project site versus about 14 mJ and about 30 mJ elsewhere; pulse duration below 5 ns versus 7 ns in a pre-flight document); the primary Wiens et al. (2012) Body Unit paper was not read. The ChemCam landing date (August 2012) comes from a secondary summary. The SuperCam Body Unit paper excerpt read does not give a LIBS-laser pulse duration or LIBS-only mass and power. The SuperCam Mast Unit paper (Maurice et al., 2021) was identified but not read. MarSCoDe values come from a supplementary information file; the primary design paper (Xu et al., 2021) was not read in full, and its mass, power and temperature range are not publicly specified in the sources read. Zhurong operational dates and end-of-mission status were not verified in a primary source. The Chandrayaan-2 LIBS is classed as not operated on the lunar surface based on news coverage of the lander loss. The Chandrayaan-2 paper title describes a mid-UV to visible instrument while its laser wavelength is 1540 nm; the spectral range is given as both 220-800 nm and 190-800 nm; the mass is given as 1.1 kg and 1.2 kg. The Chandrayaan-3 LIBS has no laser, spectrometer, mass, power or dimension values in the sources read, no primary instrument paper, and only preliminary element results. The ISRO-linked references give no peer-reviewed instrument paper for the Chandrayaan-3 LIBS. The article does not recommend lunar landing sites and does not assert any lander or rover compatibility.

data_quality_notes: Chandrayaan-2 LIBS status: flight model built and integrated into the rover (Current Science 2020) but lunar surface operation is not reported; lander loss is based on September 2019 news coverage (Planetary Society). ISRO's own statements on the loss were not read.

Chandrayaan-3 Pragyan LIBS: operation on the lunar surface is reported by ISRO (28 August 2023) and by a secondary news article. No laser, spectrometer, mass, power or dimension values were found, and no peer-reviewed or technical instrument paper was identified. Its LIBS specifications are null.
Chandrayaan-3 LIBS design relationship: whether the Chandrayaan-3 unit shares the Chandrayaan-2 design is not confirmed.

ChemCam laser pulse energy conflicts across sources: greater than 10 mJ (project site, used here), about 14 mJ (older mission summary) and about 30 mJ (secondary article). Pulse duration: less than 5 ns (project site, used here) versus 7 ns (pre-flight document). The primary Wiens et al. (2012) Body Unit paper was not read.
ChemCam mass, power and dimensions are not publicly specified in the sources read. The SuperCam paper states only that SuperCam has almost the same mass as ChemCam.

ChemCam landing date (August 2012) and the figure of more than 600 targets in two years come from secondary summaries and were not verified in a primary source. The target count is not used as a specification.

ChemCam project site (msl-chemcam.com): the cited page was read through WebFetch; the clean site root returned HTTP 200 on a later check. The cited page is recorded in references[ref_11] by its page identifier, with the query parameter removed from the stored URL.

SuperCam: the LIBS-laser pulse duration is not stated in the Body Unit paper excerpt read, and LIBS-only mass and power are not given. The mast and body unit masses and powers are whole-hardware values, not LIBS-only values.
SuperCam Mast Unit paper (Maurice et al., 2021) was identified via DOI but not read in full; its LIBS specifications, if different from the Body Unit paper, are unverified.

MarSCoDe: laser and spot values come from a secondary supplementary information file (Liu, Ling et al., 2022), not from the primary design paper (Xu et al., 2021), which was not read in full. Working-distance lower bounds vary between sources (1.5, 1.6 and 1.7 m). The 1064 nm laser value agrees with a second secondary search summary but was not checked against the primary paper.

MarSCoDe mass, power, dimensions and temperature limits are not publicly specified in the sources read. The statement about solar power limiting temperature control comes from secondary search summaries and is not used as a specification.
Zhurong operational dates and end-of-mission status were not verified in a primary source; the article does not state them.

Chandrayaan-2 LIBS spectral range is given as 220-800 nm (Table 1) and 190-800 nm (Table 2 spectrograph); both are recorded as printed. The title describes a mid-UV to visible instrument, while the laser wavelength is 1540 nm.
Chandrayaan-2 LIBS mass is given as about 1.1 kg (abstract, Table 1) and as a 1.2 kg requirement (introduction). Both are recorded.

Chandrayaan-2 values were read from text extraction of the PDF (Current Science, vol. 118, no. 4). Some symbols were lost in extraction (for example the micro sign and the degree sign). Slit dimensions are recorded as 50 x 500 (units inferred as micrometres from the table layout); this inference should be checked against the printed table.

The ISRO LIBS page and the Spectroscopy Online article give no peer-reviewed reference for the Chandrayaan-3 LIBS. A 2020 Current Science paper that describes the Chandrayaan-2 instrument is not a Chandrayaan-3 instrument paper.

Catalogue boundary: catalogue 075 (Laser-induced plasma spectrometer) describes a closely related technique. This article does not decide whether 060 and 075 should be separated or merged; the catalogue is treated as immutable for this workflow.

Image rights: NASA images are published under NASA media usage terms; credit lines are reproduced as given on the NASA Photojournal pages. No public-domain status is asserted. The jpl.nasa.gov mirror pages returned HTTP 403 to automated access, so science.nasa.gov Photojournal pages are cited as source pages.
No full-resolution download was checked. Image asset URLs were verified as HTTP 200 image/jpeg responses only.

Lunar concepts and proposals: other lunar LIBS concepts appeared in search results but were not read; none is included in the article or JSON because no verified specifications or interface evidence was reviewed.
No lander or rover compatibility is asserted for any lunar LIBS example. The Chandrayaan-2 interface description is a design description, not verified compatibility evidence.
